title: Highest Salary Jobs: How to Compare Hourly Rates, Annual Pay, and Casual Loading with Super
description: Learn how to convert hourly rates to annual pay for the highest salary jobs in Australia. Understand casual loading, superannuation, and tax for 38-hour weeks.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, an hourly rate of $50 yields an annual gross of $98,800, with super of $11,856 paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I calculate annual pay from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by hours per week (typically 38) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $30/hour × 38 × 52 = $59,280 gross per year. This assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an additional 25% on the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of leave entitlements. The National Minimum Wage casual rate is $33.05/hour (including loading). Super is paid on the total casual earnings, and our calculator adds the loading automatically when you check the box.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in my salary or paid on top?
faqs.a: Super is paid on top of your base salary or hourly earnings. For a $90,000 base salary, the employer contributes an additional $10,800 (at 12%) to your super fund, not included in your take-home pay. A total remuneration package includes super inside it, so you must divide by 1.12 to find the taxable salary.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Hourly to Annual Conversion for the Highest Salary Jobs

When you're evaluating job offers or planning your career, knowing how to convert an hourly rate to annual pay is essential. This is especially true for the highest salary jobs, where the difference between a base salary and a total remuneration package can be significant. In Australia, most full-time roles are based on a 38-hour week, and the standard formula is simple: hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks.

For example, if you earn $50 per hour and work 38 hours each week, your annual gross pay is $50 × 38 × 52 = $98,800. This figure does not include superannuation, which is paid on top by your employer. To see your take-home pay, you need to deduct income tax and the Medicare levy. The [the timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your hourly rate and instantly see the annual equivalent, including casual loading if applicable.

### The Role of Casual Loading

Many of the highest salary jobs in industries like construction, hospitality, and healthcare offer casual employment. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on their base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave entitlements. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that this loading is added to the minimum pay rate. For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $33.05 per hour, which includes the 25% loading on the base $26.44 rate.

When using our calculator, you can check the "casual loading" box to add 25% on top of your base hourly rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes loading; the calculator handles it for you. This ensures your annual estimate reflects the correct casual earnings.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top, Not Inside

A common mistake when comparing the highest salary jobs is confusing a base salary with a total remuneration package. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For a $98,800 annual gross, your employer would contribute an additional $11,856 to your super fund. This is not part of your take-home pay.

The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page explains how to compare offers correctly. If a job is advertised as a $110,000 package including super, your taxable salary is actually about $98,214 (dividing by 1.12). The wagecalculator.au salary comparison tool demonstrates that take-home pay can differ significantly when you strip out super.

### Tax and Medicare

For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are: nil on the first $18,200, 15% on income up to $45,000, 30% up to $135,000, 37% up to $190,000, and 45% above that. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. Using the $98,800 example, your tax would be approximately $19,020 and Medicare $1,976, leaving a take-home of about $77,804. The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) topic provides more detail.

### Award Rates and the National Minimum Wage

Not all jobs are covered by an award, but many of the highest salary jobs fall under modern awards that set minimum rates for classifications. The Fair Work Commission reviews these rates annually. The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by any award or agreement. As of 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. Casual employees get $33.05 per hour.

The [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page lists current rates. For award-specific pay, use the [pay guides](/blog) or the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay Calculator. The pay calculator also sources live award rates from the Fair Work Commission database.

### Comparing Job Offers: Hourly vs Salary

When you're looking at the highest salary jobs, you might receive an offer as an hourly rate or an annual salary. To compare fairly, convert both to the same basis. If you have an hourly rate, multiply by 38 and 52 to get annual gross. If you have a salary, check whether it includes super. The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool helps you switch between the two.

Also consider the hours you'll actually work. A $100,000 salary for a 50-hour week gives a lower hourly rate than a $90,000 salary for 38 hours. The wagecalculator.au example shows that take-home per hour can be $29.80 vs $35.77, so the smaller salary may be better value.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross, multiply your weekly pay by 2. For a $98,800 annual salary, weekly is $1,900, so fortnightly is $3,800. After tax and Medicare, your fortnightly take-home would be around $2,992. This is useful for budgeting.

### Annualised Wages and Offsetting

Some awards allow annualised wages, where you receive a fixed amount that covers penalties, overtime, and allowances. The Fair Work Ombudsman notes that these arrangements must be reviewed annually to ensure the employee received at least the award minimum. If you're in a role with an annualised wage, your hourly rate may not be straightforward. Always check the award rules.

### Summary

To evaluate the highest salary jobs, start with the hourly rate, assume 38 hours per week, multiply by 52, add super on top, and then deduct tax. Use the [the timesheet](/) to run your own numbers. Remember that casual loading adds 25% to the base rate, and super is separate from your salary. By understanding these components, you can make informed decisions about job offers and career moves.
